title: How a browser extension reaches the page
purpose: Show which part of an extension touches the page and why the manifest permissions decide what it can see.
explanation: The manifest declares the extension parts and the permissions they get. A content script runs in the page and reads or changes the DOM. A DevTools page adds a panel to DevTools. Both send messages to the background script, which holds shared state, and a popup or panel shows the result. Every tool in your toolkit uses this same structure, so its permissions tell you what data it can read.
alt: Flowchart: manifest.json with permissions and host access points to the background script, the content script and the DevTools page. The content script reads and changes the page DOM and sends messages to the background script. The DevTools page also sends messages to the background script, which feeds a popup or panel that shows results.

learning_check.question: An accessibility extension must read the headings on every page you open. Which part of the extension does that, and what in the manifest allows it?
learning_check.answer: A content script reads the page DOM. Host permissions (or matches for the content script) in manifest.json decide on which sites it may run.

title: Parts of a WebExtension and who talks to whom
purpose: Show the parts that manifest.json can declare and which of them touch the page.
explanation: manifest.json is the only required file. It points to the background script, content scripts, popup, sidebar and options pages, and web accessible resources. A content script works on the page DOM and talks to the background script by messages. It talks to page scripts only through window.postMessage. Popups, sidebars and options pages can use the same privileged APIs as the background script.
alt: Flowchart: manifest.json points to a background script, a content script, popup sidebar and options pages, and web accessible resources. The content script reads and changes the page DOM, sends messages to the background script and uses window.postMessage to reach page scripts. Popup, sidebar and options pages use the same APIs as the background script.

learning_check.question: How can a content script ask the browser to run an API it is not allowed to call itself?
learning_check.answer: It sends a message to the background script, which can use any API its permissions allow.

title: How Google crawls, renders and indexes a JavaScript page
purpose: Show that Google indexes the rendered HTML, so a tool must show you the page after JavaScript ran.
explanation: Googlebot checks robots.txt, fetches the raw HTML and queues pages with status 200 for rendering. A headless Chromium then runs the JavaScript. Google indexes the rendered HTML. A page blocked in robots.txt is never rendered, so an SEO extension that reads only the source HTML misses what Google sees.
alt: Flowchart: a URL in the crawl queue is checked against robots.txt. If blocked it is skipped. If allowed, raw HTML is fetched, pages with status 200 are queued for rendering, a headless Chromium runs the JavaScript, and the rendered HTML is indexed.

learning_check.question: Which HTML does Google index, and what happens to a URL that robots.txt disallows?
learning_check.answer: Google indexes the rendered HTML. A disallowed URL is skipped and its JavaScript is not rendered.

title: axe-core module map
purpose: Show the six analyzed parts of axe-core and which part calls which.
explanation: The engine run is the centre. It starts a frame job for iframes and runs every rule on this page. Rules call small checks, such as heading order and colour contrast. Tests guard the engine, and the build ships one bundle that CI tests. Accessibility extensions wrap this engine.
alt: Flowchart: engine-run points to frame-messaging for iframe jobs, to the headings and landmarks rules for any, all and none checks, and to the color-contrast check. A tests node points to engine-run with a dotted line, and the build node points to engine-run as the shipped bundle.

learning_check.question: Which part of axe-core handles iframes, and which part decides if text contrast is enough?
learning_check.answer: Frame messaging handles iframes. The colour-contrast check, called by the engine run, decides contrast.

title: One axe.run call from start to report
purpose: Show how one scan moves through the engine and where a check can answer 'cannot tell'.
explanation: The caller starts a scan. The engine sets a running flag, builds the page context, and queues two jobs: scan child frames and run the rules here. Each rule runs checks per element. A check returns true, false or undefined. The engine merges results, runs the after step, builds the report, and resets the flag.
alt: Sequence diagram: the caller calls axe.run, run.js sets the running flag and calls runRules, which queues a frame job and a rule job. Rules run any, all and none checks that return true, false or undefined. Results are merged, finalized, reported to the caller and the engine is reset.

learning_check.question: What are the three possible answers of a check, and which one means a person must look?
learning_check.answer: True, false and undefined. Undefined is reported as incomplete and needs human review.
